content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an unsupervised method for learning 'hierarchical 3D representations' from 2D images. The proposed network is called IGC-Net. It first extracts global shape and appearance features and then decomposes them into part-level depth and appearance features. These features are decomposed to depth, albedo, and pose information, and then compose and relight to a face image. The experiment shows the model is able to discover major facial components for recognition, and it outperforms previous works on unsupervised face segmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ Compare with previous works, the paper proposes a method that incorporates 3D information, which directly benefits the method in segmenting faces with large-scale poses. 
+ The L_{contra} term promises the semantic consistency of each part among all the instances. This is new in this line of work.
+ The performance is better than the previous methods quantitatively and qualitatively. 

Weakness:
+ The lighting and rendering part is unclear. As 3D is a major component of this method, the paper didn't point out what rendering method it uses, and how the lighting is decomposed.
+ The position parameterization is unclear. It is only pointed out in Figure 1 that the parameter could be row-yaw-pitch. It's better to state it clearly in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
+ Hierarchical: The concept of hierarchy in the title is unclear to me. I personally think hierarchy should refer to a more complicated structure. The method only has two levels - part and global. Is the model able to solve multiple levels of detail?

+ Lighting and rendering: As I stated before, the paper should provide more detail about the lighting and rendering part to make it self-contained. 

+ Figure 2: In the gray box, should it be "hard softmax" instead of "softmax"?

+ M_{MXD}: Is there any constraint pervent any row of M_{MXD} matric become  an all zero row?

+ Equation 7: Having a symmetric loss could potentially improve the model. However, the human face might have different facial expressions making it non-symmetric. I'm wondering about the performance when removing the symmetric term.

+ L_{contra}: For contrastive loss, the batch size is an important factor that affects performance. What is the batch size the paper adopts?

+ M: The paper uses M=6 for the experiments. I'm wondering how the model will segment faces with different numbers of M. I think the result from different numbers of M will provide intellectually interesting results on face analysis. 

+ Pose parameter: What pose parameter is adopted in this paper? If the paper only adopts rotation parameters, is rotation without translation enough to represent faces that might appear at any position in an image? 

+ Dataset: This is only a suggestion, and it doesn't affect my rating of this paper. The paper only shows results on the human face dataset, but as a general unsupervised method, it will be better to show results on more general categories of objects like SCOPS.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper looks into the unsupervised segmentation of images from a 3D perspective, and the performance is better than previous methods. However, several major components in the paper are unclear. I'm willing to raise the score if the author can respond and resolve my concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies capsule networks to learn hierarchical 3D face representations from 2D images.  It proposes an Inverse Graphics Capsule Network (IGC-Net) to learn 3D primitives with interpretable parameters, and therefore it could reconstruct human faces in a bottom-up hierarchical manner.  In addition, those learned 3D primitives could show appealing semantic consistency, because those face images are naturally decomposed into semantic-consistent parts: background, eyes, mouth, forehead, nose, and cheek without direct supervision. They evaluated the proposed method on CelebA, BP4D, and Multi-PIE datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. It is interesting to use a capsule network to learn hierarchical 3D face representations, which shows good semantic-consistency feature decomposition.
2. The silhouettes of 3D parts could be utilized in the unsupervised face segmentation task.

Weaknesses:
The limited novelty and contribution of this work are my major concern.  The capsule network has already been used for 2D face analysis, such as the work[1]; and unsupervised 3d face reconstruction has been achieved in many previous works, such as the work[2-4].  Therefore, this work seems to be a combination of existing methods, and the achievements seem to be straightforward. The authors are welcome to highlight research gaps and the contributions in the response. 

[1] Chang Yu, Xiangyu Zhu, Xiaomei Zhang, ZiduWang, Zhaoxiang Zhang, and Zhen Lei. Hp-capsule: Unsupervised face part discovery by hierarchical parsing capsule network. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 4032–4041, 2022.
[2] Shangzhe Wu, Christian Rupprecht, and Andrea Vedaldi. Unsupervised learning of probably symmetric deformable 3d objects from images in the wild. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 1–10, 2020.
[3] Zhenyu Zhang, Yanhao Ge, Renwang Chen, Ying Tai, Yan Yan, Jian Yang, Chengjie Wang, Jilin Li, and Feiyue Huang. Learning to aggregate and personalize 3d face from in-the-wild photo collection. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 14214–14224, 2021.
[4] Zhenyu Zhang, Yanhao Ge, Ying Tai, Weijian Cao, Renwang Chen, Kunlin Liu, Hao Tang, Xiaoming Huang, Chengjie Wang, Zhifeng Xie, et al. Physically-guided disentangled implicit rendering for 3d face modeling. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 20353–20363, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing and presentation of this manuscript are generally good. 
I am worried about the novelty as discussed in the previous section.
Perhaps, the authors could further highlight the contributions in the revised version.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, this work shows good 3D face reconstruction with a capsule network with supervised training.  However, a few features have already been achieved in existing works, making this work less novel and significant. At the current stage, I could not suggest its acceptance, but I am willing to reconsider when the other reviews and the authors' response are available.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents an inverse graphics capsule network to learn the 3D representations from 2D images in an unsupervised manner. The hierarchy of objects is represented by part capsules that represent depth, albedo, and 3D pose of the objects. Experiments on CelebA, BP4D and Multi-PIE face datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed methods in unsupervised face segmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The proposed approach is straightforward and well-illustrated.
2. Experimental comparisons show superior results to baselines.

Cons:
The major concern is that the experimental verification is quite weak.
1) The authors claim the proposed method could decompose the objects into a set of consistent semantic parts and then assembles them into object-level descriptions to build the hierarchy. It would be better to show some results for generic objects rather than just faces. Otherwise, the authors should tone down their claims.
2) The authors state that, unlike HP-Capsule, which operates in a 2D space, this work learns hierarchical 3D representations. Thus, it can handle faces with large poses. This should be supported by strong evidence provided in the experiments. 
3)  I expect to see more results coming from the learned 3D representation. It would be nice if the authors could provide more visual depth or normal results. Currently, I only see two examples.
4) If possible, the authors can add a comparison with GAN-based 3D decomposition baselines, such as GAN2Shape (ICLR' 21), and LiftedGAN (CVPR' 21). 
5) More ablation studies are needed to better the effectiveness of each component in the proposed inverse graphics capsule network and the cross-attention mechanism.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think, It is a well-written and clearly explained article overall. Its main weakness is the evaluation, in which the authors fail to support their conclusions.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a capsule based novel architecture for discovering 3D parts of faces.

- The capsules encode features from the input image.
- These features represent 3D face parts like eyses, mouth etc.
- A Graphics Decoder module turns these parts into interpretable objects with albedo depth and pose
- The parts are merged and rendered.
- An unsupervised learning scheme (Wu etal) is used to train the model in an autoencoder setup.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The idea itself is interesting and novel.

The proposed method outperformed baselines in semantic consistency metrics (e.g. tab1 tab 2)

Weaknesses:

- The proposed method has much lower visual quality than SOTA methods, e.g. pi-GAN, GRAM, GRAM-HD

pi-GAN: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.00926.pdf
GRAM: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.08867.pdf
GRAM-HD: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.07255.pdf

Capsules are usually used in a multi-stage hierarchy, but here they are only learning one level of parts.

The semantic segmentations are assessed by measuring how well the landmarks are aligned. However nowadays dense landmark correspondences can be easily extracted from models, where the appearance and shape are disentangled.
Disentangled3D:: Learning a 3D Generative Model with Disentangled Geometry and Appearance from Monocular Images, CVPR2022
The paper does not show comparisons with Disentangled3D

There are two additional losses are introduced, which look like they are fighting to get something out of the architecture, rather than the good properties (like semantic consistency) popping out naturally.
- "improve the semantic consistency across samples, we employ a contrastive loss"
- "To prevent the network from collapsing to use one capsule to describe the whole objects,
we employ the spatial sparsity..."
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is well written, easy to understand and all terms and losses etc. are defined.

Quality:

The results are far from the current SOTA. And not compared to it.

Novelty:

The idea of using capsules for unsupervised 3D and for learning 3D parts this way is novel to me.

Reproducibility:

A competent practitioner could implement it based on the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the ides presented are interesting, I recommend rejecting the paper. The comparisons are not enough to assess the merits of the approach.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses the potential of learning hierarchical 3D representations of objects under the capsule network architecture. The core idea is to apply reverse graphs to guide better decomposition of existing objects. The authors evaluate their ideas on the task of unsupervised face segmentation and demonstrate promising results both qualitatively and quantitatively on three public benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Although the idea of ​​using inverse rendering for self-supervised 3D primitive decomposition is not new and widely adopted in other fields, the authors show a good application of capsule networks, well suited for this decomposition task, and demonstrate good on performance benchmarks.

- The authors also performed a detailed ablation study, including the importance of part-level graphic capsules, to show the efficacy of other design choices.

- Qualitative results are easy to understand, showing better decompositions of this approach.

Weaknesses: 
- Some intuitions beyond design choices are unclear to me. For example, does the image need to be encoded into global shape and albedo embeddings before performing partial-level decomposition? I feel like this decomposition is performed by focusing on different parts of the global embedding, which doesn't exactly make sense to me - the global embedding may miss some information, such as part-level occlusions, so the proposed GDM sounds like is an overfitting module on learning common parts across the dataset. I think the human face is a good example, but it is probably much simpler to learn for GDM, since there are clear common patterns in the face parts. It is better to show more challenging cases, such as decomposing glasses from faces, and unsupervised learning from limited data.

- Equation 2, how are part depth, albedo, and 3D pose represented in the network? It's still unclear to me how these key designs are implemented.

- The author only shows the application of this method on a single task of unsupervised face segmentation, so the generalization ability of this method to other tasks is not clear, so I do not fully believe in the power of the proposed method.

- Minor issue, Equation 10, what is the value of \gamma in experiment?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the paper is overall clear and the presentation quality is good. This paper has some novelties in introducing capsule networks to unsupervised part segmentation. Reproducibility is not clear to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think there is something novel about this paper. However, since I still have some of the concerns listed in "Weaknesses", I tend to vote for borderline accept.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a method to learn 3D capsules (Graphics capsules) from 2D images. Different from other capsule networks, the proposed graphics capsule lives in 3D space.   Specifically, each capsule consists of depth, albedo color, and 3D pose, thereby having properties in 3D space. To learn the graphics capsules, the paper proposes a decomposition module that takes in a global embedding and outputs the set of part embeddings. From part embedding, the shared capsule decoder can output the depth, albedo color, and pose. To learn the capsules, the paper utilizes a render to reconstruct the input images. The paper validates the method in multiple face datasets and shows better reconstruction and decomposition than existing works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths:
- The capsule representation is 3D-informed, which is better aligned with human perception. And I’m also convinced this is a better way to represent capsules.

- The experimental results are better than other works. And the face recognition experiment to understand which capsule is more discriminative is very interesting to me. 

- It’s a bit surprising to me that the proposed method can work pretty well. To me, learning 3D property from a single 2D image is an ill-posed problem. But the results shown in this paper are quite impressive. 


## Weakness:
The paper has several weaknesses which I’ll detail below:

### Writing: 
In general, the writing needs to be improved a bit. I have difficulties following the method details. For examples, 
- The details of the capsule decoder are missing --e.g., how do you represent pose?
- The details of the render are missing. How do you parameterize the lighting? How do you combine lightning parameters and albedo, depth, and pose?
- The details of cross attention. In equation 6, I’m not sure if I understand how to get attention matrix M. 
- And also some design choices are not well-justified. For example, In the capsule assembling step, the method choose to use max pooling to merge albedo/depth but use averaging to merge poses. What’s the idea behind it? It might be better to justify it a bit. 

### Methods:
It’s a bit weird to perform the decomposition in the decoder. What I meant is that the global shape/albedo embedding is the latent code. And the decomposition module can be viewed as part of the decoder. In other words, the method didn’t decompose the input object in latent space. The decomposition is performed in the generated images instead. This is different from existing works. For example, in the related 3D canonical capsule [1]/flow capsules [2] (BTW, the canonical capsule is very related to this paper but missing from the related work section), the object is decomposed into parts in latent spaces. 

Nevertheless, the paper claims that the proposed capsule network decomposes the input object, which is misleading. So I strongly recommend the paper clarify the difference and justify the design choices.

[1] Sun et al. "Canonical capsules: Self-supervised capsules in the canonical pose."  NeurIPS 2021. 
[2]Sabour et al. "Unsupervised part representation by flow capsules." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.


### Experiments:
The paper claims the capsule learning in 3D. However, the method is not validated in a fair 3D setting. Specifically,
- Results on datasets that have wide camera viewpoints are missing. The datasets used in this paper are mostly about faces where the viewpoints are severely biased -- i.e., cameras pointing toward the front of the face.  In this case, it is hard to know if the method can really learn the 3D capsules from 2D images. Therefore, I would recommend using datasets like SRN cars used in PixelNerf where objects are rendered from wide camera viewpoints.
- Since this paper is about 3D capsules, I would recommend having some metrics to measure the 3D learning accuracy -- for example multi-view consistency, and camera pose accuracy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presented method to learn 3D capsules is novel. But the clarity/quality is however low as I detailed in the weakness section above. Regarding the reproducibility, I think it's not high given lots of method details are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The 3D capsule learned from 2D images is very interesting. But however, the paper has several weaknesses in terms of experimental validation and writing. Given the high bar of this conference, I tend to reject this paper. But I would like to hear from the authors during the rebuttal just in case I misunderstand anything.

content.title: Graphics Capsule: Learning hierarchical 3D representations from 2D images and its application on human faces
content.abstract: The function of constructing the hierarchy of objects is important to the visual process of the human brain. Previous studies have successfully adopted capsule networks to decompose the digits and faces into parts in an unsupervised manner to investigate the similar perception mechanism of neural networks. However, their descriptions are restricted to the 2D space, limiting their capacities to imitate the intrinsic 3D perception ability of humans. In this paper, we propose an Inverse Graphics Capsule Network (IGC-Net) to learn the hierarchical 3D representations from large-scale unlabeled images. The core of IGC-Net is a new type of capsule, named graphics capsule, which represents 3D primitives with interpretable parameters in computer graphics (CG), including depth, albedo, and 3D pose. Specifically, IGC-Net first decomposes the objects into a set of semantic-consistent parts and then assembles them to the object-level descriptions to build the hierarchy. The learned graphics capsules reveal how the neural networks, oriented at visual perception, understand objects as a hierarchy of 3D models. Besides, the discovered parts can be deployed to the unsupervised face segmentation task to evaluate the semantic consistency of our method. Moreover, the part-level descriptions with explicit physical meanings give an insight into the face analysis that originally runs in a black box, such as the importance of shape and texture for face recognition. Experiments on CelebA, BP4D, and Multi-PIE validate the effectiveness of our method.
